asSun.p: The Sun rules Leo and Strength is Leo's card, so if you've got a Leo Sun this one is yours by default, the same way an Aries gets The Emperor. Look at the picture for a second. A woman has both hands on a lion's jaw. There's no rope, she's not wearing armour, and she doesn't look like she's working very hard. That's what strength means in Leo. An Aries would be wrestling the animal. A Capricorn would have built a fence. You don't need either, because you've got enough warmth in you that the lion settles on its own. The fixed fire part matters too. Leo doesn't flare up and burn out. It's the kind of fire that's still going when you come down in the morning, and people pick that up about you quickly, usually in the first five minutes.

Day to day it comes out as needing to mean what you do. You can't work at half heart for long, you either put the whole of yourself into a thing or you quietly drift off it, and there isn't much in between. You stay loyal well past the point where other people would have left. You've also got real pride, and you know the exact second it's been touched. What happens in that second is the interesting bit. There's a pause where you decide whether pride gets to answer or you do. You've probably had that pause a few thousand times by now, and it's got longer as you've got older.

Your confidence rubs off on people. You so obviously expect the people around you to be good that they tend to be, and I mean that literally, people do better work and tell better jokes when you're in the room. The other thing, which is rarer, is that you can stay warm towards someone who's being a pain. Most people go cold or go sharp. You just keep the temperature where it was and wait. Kids and dogs and nervous new staff all settle near you for the same reason. None of it costs you much either, which is probably why you don't rate it as highly as you should.

Your pride likes to dress up as composure. Because you're proud of being the steady one, you'll refuse to admit something hurt you, and then punish the person slowly with a cooler version of yourself for about a week. A Leo Sun that isn't appreciated doesn't always roar. Quite often it sulks, with tremendous dignity, and everyone can tell. The other trap is needing to be seen being strong, so even your patience starts to have an audience in mind. You can usually feel when you've crossed into that. When you have, the fix is boring. Say you're cross. Out loud, in plain words, to the person it's about.

Leo's natural house is the fifth, which is romance and play and children, so you love the way a Leo does anything: properly, in the open, with a bit of show to it. You court. You remember what they said about their sister three months ago. You want them to feel picked in front of other people. What you want back is to be admired out loud, and you're a bit shy of admitting that. Admit it anyway. Nobody guesses that the capable one needs applause. When you're hurt, your first move is to go regal and distant, which your partner reads as cold. Let them see it while it still stings, even if all you manage is 'that hurt'.

You need your name on something. It doesn't have to be famous, a few people reading it is enough, but anonymous work drains you faster than hard work does. You lead well because people feel safe under you. You take the blame upward and pass the credit down, and you hardly ever need to raise your voice. Where it goes wrong is pride. You take on the project that's sinking because you can't stand to watch it sink, and then you won't ask for help. You also stay too long. Fixed fire hates to quit, so I'd check in with yourself once a year about whether you still like this job or you're just loyal to it.

Next time your pride gets stung, in a meeting, in a text, whatever it is, put one hand flat on your breastbone and take three slow breaths before you answer. Then say one true sentence, something like 'that landed badly for me'. Don't go cold and don't go loud, just say the sentence. Try it once this week on something small. A comment about your parking is fine.

asMoon.p: The Moon doesn't make its own light, it shines with what the Sun gives it, and in Leo it's sitting in the Sun's own sign. So your feelings have borrowed the Sun's manner. They're warm, they're proud, and because Leo is fixed fire they take a while to catch and a lot longer to go out. The Moon has no particular dignity in Leo, by the way. It's a guest there, and the host is the Sun, and that's pretty much what it feels like from inside. Strength is Leo's card, and as a Moon card it's about what you do with a feeling once it's arrived. Notice the woman on the card isn't muzzling the lion. She's got her hands on it and she's staying. That's the skill this placement is either born with or born needing, and I've seen both.

Your moods are whole-body events. When you're happy you're generous and a bit loud, and when you're hurt you go very quiet and very upright. Leo being a fixed sign, nothing passes through you fast. You can still feel a slight from 2011 at close to full heat, and you can still feel a kindness from the same year, which is the nicer half of the same trait. You need the house to be warm in the literal sense, sunlight, colour, someone pleased to see you at the door. And you keep your dignity about pain. The people closest to you usually find out you were struggling after you've already dealt with it, which they don't love.

You make people feel they're allowed to be big. Someone crying in your kitchen never gets the sense they're too much, because you sorted that out with your own feelings years ago and large ones don't frighten you. Your affection is physical and steady. It's the hand on the shoulder, the meal that turns up, the very fierce phone call on behalf of whoever's been treated badly. Children trust a Leo Moon quickly, because you take their dramas seriously without panicking about them. It's the same with adults, honestly. People come to you with the thing they haven't told anyone, and they're usually right to.

A Leo Moon needs to be wanted, and the problem is how proud you are about that. You'd sooner go without comfort than ask for it and get a lukewarm answer. So you test people instead. You go quiet, you wait to see who notices, and you keep score when they don't, and I've watched that go on for months. Hurt pride can sit in you a long time looking a lot like calm. There's also a hardness you keep for yourself. You'll forgive a friend a whole bad week and then call your own upset childish, or attention-seeking, or whatever word your family used for it. It isn't. It's a need, and a fairly reasonable one.

In love you need affection you can actually see and hear. Being told, being touched, being picked first. For you that's food, and a reserved partner can love you completely and still leave you hungry, so it's worth saying early on what warmth looks like to you, in specifics. You give the old-fashioned kind of devotion and you're very hard to drive off. The sore spot is being laughed at, or brushed aside, right after you've shown something soft. When that happens you go polite. Good manners, closed door. Tell them instead, the same day if you can manage it, even if all you get out is 'that stung'.

Your feelings come to work with you whatever the job description says. You do well where there's some heart in the task and someone notices what you did, and you wilt in places that are cold or grudging or sarcastic, even when the money's good. I'd pay attention to how much one thank-you lifts your whole week. That's useful information about what you need. In a tense team you're the one who can sit with the upset colleague, or the furious client, and bring the temperature down. Just check at the end of the day that you haven't spent all of it settling other people and then driven home with your own stuff untouched.

Once this week, ask for comfort out loud before anyone's had a chance to guess. Keep it small and exact. 'I've had a rough day, can I have a hug', or 'tell me one thing I did well today'. You'll feel a flash of pride that says you shouldn't have to ask. Let it go past and ask anyway. The people who love you have usually been waiting for a way in.

asRising.p: Your rising sign is whatever was coming up over the eastern horizon the minute you were born. It sets the first house, which is the body, how you carry yourself, how you start things. With Leo there the Sun ends up ruling your whole chart, and Leo's card, Strength, becomes the card people meet at the door. Look at how the woman stands. Nothing in her hands, no armour, and a lion right next to her that she clearly isn't worried about. That's the posture Leo rising gives you, whether or not you feel it on the day. Fixed fire at the front of the chart means strangers get a steady warmth off you first, long before they get your history or any of your doubts, and a lot of them never get past that first bit.

It's in the body before it's in anything you say. Leo rising usually carries itself well, chest open, a walk that takes up its fair share of the footpath, and often some flourish in the hair or the clothes. You start things wholeheartedly or you don't start them, and you're bad at slipping into a room unnoticed even when you'd really like to. Strangers give you attention you didn't ask for. They also assume you're more confident than you actually are, which can be lonely. Under pressure your instinct is to slow down and get warmer, where most people speed up and get sharp, and that's worth knowing about yourself.

People decide within about a minute that they can hand you something, and they're usually right. You walk into a tense room, a nervous class, your partner's family mid-argument, and your ease gives everyone a lower gear to drop into. Because the Sun rules your chart, your life tends to go better when you let yourself be seen. Hiding costs you more energy than showing up does, which is the opposite of how it works for a lot of people. You're also good with things that are wary of you. The snappy dog, the sullen fifteen-year-old, the new client who's been burnt before. You don't crowd them and you don't back off, and sooner or later they come over.

A calm face this convincing turns into a job after a while. You start to feel you're not allowed an off day, because everyone's cast you as the unshakeable one and you half agreed to it. Then the gap between the face and what's behind it gets wider, and nobody thinks to ask how you're going, because why would they. Leo rising also bruises when it's ignored. Being overlooked at the door, talked across in a meeting, left off an invitation, all of that stings far more than it should and you'd hate anyone to see that it does. Warmth that has to be noticed starts turning into a performance. You can feel the difference even when nobody else can.

People fall for the glow first and meet the actual person second, so a lot of your work in love is slowing that down. Let someone see you with the lights off. Tired, unsure, not hosting. With Leo on the first house, Aquarius lands on your seventh, the house of partners, and you tend to be pulled towards cooler, more independent people who have no intention of orbiting you. That's good for you, even when it's annoying. They give you room, you give them warmth, it works. The only real trouble starts when you read their need for space as a verdict on you, and it very rarely is one.

You get given the front-of-house job whether or not you applied for it. The presentation, the difficult customer, the speech at the farewell drinks. You're good at it, and first impressions do real work for you in interviews and pitches, so use that and don't feel bad about it. What to guard against is being hired for your presence and then coasting on it, and letting colleagues assume you're fine under pressure because you look fine. Say when the load's too much. And give yourself time to prepare where nobody can see you doing it. The ease people admire holds up a lot better when you've actually done the reading the night before.

Before you walk into any room that matters this week, stop at the door for one breath. Shoulders down, jaw loose, and ask yourself whether you're about to perform warm or be warm. If it's the first, pick one person in there to be genuinely curious about and start with them. Then, once this week, answer 'how are you' honestly to someone safe. It'll feel strange the first time.

asBirthCard.p: This card doesn't come from your Sun or your Moon or anything else in the chart. It comes from your birthdate. Add up every digit, and if the total goes over 22 add those digits again, and you land on eight, which is Strength. Eight sits between The Chariot, which wins by pushing, and The Hermit, which goes off alone, and it's the card in the middle where you learn to handle something without doing either. It's also four doubled, so it's structure that's been through something and got built again. Turn the numeral on its side and you've got the loop floating over the woman's head on the card. Eight comes round again and again. It's a number about stamina, and what it's picked out in you is that you can keep coming back to the same hard thing without going stale on it.

As a lifelong pattern, eight turns up as the same test wearing different clothes. Every few years there's something with teeth in it. A difficult boss, a relative who blows up at Christmas, a fear you thought you'd dealt with, an appetite that wants to run the house. Every time, the blunt approach fails and the patient one works, and every time you seem to have to learn that from scratch, which is a bit maddening. You're probably at your best in the long middle of things too, after the excitement has worn off and before anything's finished, right where most people lose heart. That's your stretch, and you might as well plan around it.

What you get out of all that is a strength that builds on itself. Someone who has calmed the same beast a dozen times stops being scared of it. By your forties an eight person usually has an unusual tolerance for intensity, their own and everyone else's, and a reputation for being good in a crisis without making a thing of it. You're hard to provoke and hard to wear down. There's a quieter gift under that. You understand, from the inside, that wild things respond to respect, and that includes wild people. So you end up being the one who gets on with the colleague or the horse or the teenager everyone else has written off.

The loop can run the wrong way. Because you're good at enduring, you endure things you should have left. The job that drains you, the friendship where you do all the ringing, the situation you keep calming that never actually calms. Patience becomes a way of avoiding the harder job of saying no. The other side of it is control. Once you've learnt to manage your own temper and your own appetites, you start managing everyone's, reading every room for risk, never quite sitting back in the chair. And when you do slip, lose it, give in, you're brutal with yourself about it. Far harder than you'd ever be on a friend who did the same thing.

In relationships you're the one who stays level when it gets loud, and partners lean on that, sometimes very hard. It's a real strength. Have a look, though, at whether you keep choosing people who need calming. The pattern can quietly make you the permanent handler, so love ends up feeling like a job you happen to be good at. You're allowed someone who looks after you back. Be the unreasonable one now and then. Be the one who's scared, or furious, or needs a lift from the airport at midnight, and see what your partner does with it. If they can't do it, that's worth knowing early.

You suit anything where long patience with something alive or volatile pays off. Teaching, nursing, training animals, managing people, negotiating, rehab work, slow craft. You're the one who gets handed the account nobody else could keep, and you keep it. Eight is also the number of doing the same thing again and again, so your skills come through practice and you shouldn't measure yourself against the quick starters in the office. They peak early. The risk for you is absorbing too much. Because you can take pressure, more of it gets sent your way, and it keeps coming until you say something. Say something while the load is still a choice, and don't apologise when you do.

Pick the one thing that keeps testing you, a person, a habit, a fear, and for one week meet it at the same time each day for five minutes and no longer. Five minutes drafting the hard conversation. Five minutes sitting with the craving before you decide. Five minutes on the task you've been dodging. Then stop, even if it's going well, especially then. At the end of the week write down one line about whether the thing looks any smaller.
